name: kawa
desc: Programming language for Java (implementation of Scheme)
why: A Scheme implementation targeting the JVM is a genuinely odd meeting of Lisp and Java bytecode worth an afternoon.

brief.what_it_is: Kawa is a general-purpose programming language that runs on the Java platform, implemented as an extension of Scheme, a Lisp-family language. It takes Scheme source code, either interactively in a REPL or as scripts or compiled code, and runs it on the JVM. The manual also describes it as a framework for implementing other languages on the Java platform, with many utility classes. The brew executable is named kawa.
brief.why_it_exists: The manual says Kawa aims to combine the benefits of dynamic scripting languages (non-verbose code, fast and easy startup, a REPL, no required compilation step) with those of traditional compiled languages (fast execution, static error detection, modularity, zero-overhead Java platform integration).
brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond the brew formula name and executable was found in the pages I read. The manual has a 'Getting and installing Kawa' section, but I did not fetch it, so I have no install steps, runtime requirements beyond the Java platform, or first-run details.
brief.standout: Scheme on the JVM with the stated goal of making scripting-style quick starts and a REPL coexist with compiled speed and Java integration. Kawa is also pitched as a base for building other languages on the JVM, not only as a Scheme.
brief.status: Quiet, with weak evidence. The manual says it describes version 3.1.1, updated 16 January 2020. I found no later release date or recent commit in what I fetched, so I can't confirm it is actively maintained.
brief.caveats: The first homepage fetch returned only a fragment of diff-style markup, not the page text, so I used the index.html page instead. I did not see a GitHub README or any command examples. The manual calls its tutorial 'woefully incomplete'. The project says it has nothing to do with the defunct Kawa commercial Java IDE, which is worth noting to avoid confusion.
quotes: Kawa is a general-purpose programming language that runs on the Java platform.
It is an extension of the long-established Scheme language, which is in the Lisp family of programming languages.
Kawa is also a useful framework for implementing other programming languages on the Java platform.

judge.reason: Scheme compiled for the JVM is an unusual bridge between Lisp and Java, and Kawa’s role as a framework for other JVM languages gives it more to explore than a routine implementation.

entry.title: Kawa
entry.tldr: Kawa is a Scheme implementation for the Java platform: a Lisp REPL on the JVM that also compiles to bytecode and works with Java classes.
entry.deeper_look:
Kawa is a general-purpose programming language that runs on the Java platform. It is an extension of Scheme, a long-established member of the Lisp family. You can type Scheme into a REPL, run it as a script, or compile it, and it all runs on the JVM.

The manual states the aim directly: combine the benefits of dynamic scripting languages (non-verbose code, fast and easy startup, a REPL, no required compilation step) with those of traditional compiled languages (fast execution, static error detection, modularity, zero-overhead Java platform integration). Whether it fully gets there is for you to judge, but the goal explains why it exists.

The idea underneath is that a language can be a thin, flexible layer over a big runtime. The manual also calls Kawa "a useful framework for implementing other programming languages on the Java platform", with many utility classes. That makes it a door into how languages get built on the JVM, not only a place to write Scheme.

The project says it has nothing to do with the defunct Kawa commercial Java IDE, so ignore older search results about that.
entry.install:
brew install kawa
# depends on openjdk, which brew installs as a dependency

try_this.what_happens: Prints the command-line options, a good first look at how Kawa runs interactively, runs scripts, or compiles.

entry.whats_unique: It is Scheme that treats the Java platform as its home, and it is also pitched as a toolkit for building other JVM languages.
entry.caveats: The manual describes version 3.1.1, updated January 2020, and I could not confirm recent maintenance; its own tutorial is called 'woefully incomplete'.
